notes.trap: `/` always returns a fractional result, even for two integers. Under the default non-ANSI mode, dividing by zero returns NULL instead of raising an error. Use `div(...)` when you want integer division.

The remainder takes the sign of the dividend, as in Java, so a negative left operand gives a negative result. Use `pmod(...)` when you need a non-negative modulus. With ANSI off, `x % 0` returns NULL.
With ANSI mode off (the default), integer addition silently wraps around on overflow instead of raising an error. Use `try_add(...)` to get NULL on overflow, or cast to BIGINT or DECIMAL first.
INT * INT stays INT, and with ANSI off an overflow silently wraps to a wrong value instead of failing. Cast an operand to BIGINT first, or use `try_multiply(...)`.
Subtracting two DATEs returns a day-time INTERVAL, not an integer day count. Use `datediff(...)` when you need a number.
With ANSI off, the absolute value of the minimum INT (or BIGINT) overflows and returns the same negative value. It does not raise an error or widen the type.
An argument outside [-1, 1] returns NaN, not NULL and not an error, so `IS NULL` checks will not catch it. `asin(...)` and `atanh(...)` behave the same way.
The argument order is (y, x), y first. Writers coming from Excel-style atan2(x, y) often swap the arguments.
The input is cast to BIGINT before conversion, so fractional values are truncated, not rounded. Negative numbers give a 64-bit two's-complement string.
`bround(...)` uses HALF_EVEN (banker's) rounding, unlike `round(...)` which uses HALF_UP. Ties therefore go to the even digit.
Without a scale argument, `ceil(...)` on a DOUBLE returns BIGINT, not DOUBLE. Values beyond the BIGINT range are lost.
A negative input with a positive target base is treated as an unsigned 64-bit two's-complement value. Pass a negative `to_base` to get signed output.
